title: Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs
author: Will DePue (Unemployment Labs)
updated_note: within about nine hours of publication (archived copies from 12 November 21:56 UTC to 13 November 06:59 UTC) the GPU-count estimates were revised twice, a DeepSeek-V3 sanity check of that arithmetic was removed, and "available to reviewers on request" became a public code repository; the report labels the revision 12 November (US time), and nothing has changed since
takeaway: A forensic report with public code: it regenerates embedding rows that training never touched from a recovered seed and finds they line up only under one GPU thread count (2,048 threads per SM times the SM count), so six open-weight models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group released April to November 2026 read as initialised on Blackwell-class layouts (148 or 152 SMs) where the same labs' earlier models read as Hopper (132); by the report's own scoping this identifies the hardware class that created the starting weights, not where the chips were, who owned them, whether the whole run used them, or whether any law was broken.
verdict: Believe the mechanism and the readings: the untouched rows match to a correlation above 0.9999 only at one layout, the code is public, an outside reimplementation recovered the same seeds blind within hours, and our own CPU replay reproduces three of them. Treat "initialised on" becoming "trained on" as a strong inference the weights cannot prove, the chip names as inferred from a thread count, and the GPU counts and costs as soft estimates that were revised twice on launch day.

headline.k: DeepSeek-V4-Flash and -Pro, Kimi K3 and K3.1-Pro, MiniMax-M3 and Ling-3.1-flash, released April to November 2026; the same four labs' earlier models read as Hopper
headline.at: Six models from four Chinese labs read as Blackwell-trained

headline.k: DeepSeek-V4-Flash's untouched embedding rows regenerated by unmodified PyTorch on a B300 (445 bit for bit); an H100 reproduced none, and the seed plus one reproduced none
headline.d: the author's hardware run; our CPU replay also gives 461 of 469

headline.k: every model whose developer named its hardware reads consistently (Llama 3.1 at 132 SMs, Pythia at 108, Nemotron-3 Ultra at 152); related models share initialisations, so this is a consistency check, not an accuracy rate
headline.d: Appendix 2, as the report itself says
headline.at: our forensic method agrees with every one

code.n: Released 13 November 05:39 UTC, about eight hours after the report: a numpy model of PyTorch's CUDA normal_ (Philox4x32-10), the released rows of DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Kimi K3, MiniMax-M3 and Ling-3.1-flash (7 MB, hashed against pinned Hugging Face revisions), a CPU replay that sweeps every SM count from 16 to 256, and a script that repeats the check with stock PyTorch on whatever GPU it runs on. One commit; no issues filed by 27 November.

more_note: Read the investigation and limits sections (about 10 minutes) before the findings; Appendix 1 holds each lab's readings over time and Appendix 2 all 50-odd models with their disclosed hardware.

discussion.t: Hacker News: Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs

responses.n: Written from PyTorch's source and posted about 85 minutes after the report, before the author's code. A blind search of all 2^32 seeds finds one hit per model at the report's layouts: V4-Flash at the report's seed, MiniMax-M3 (2760) and Ling-3.1-flash (3952), seeds the report never printed. It also reads V4-Pro and K3.1-Pro from untouched rows (1,831 and 317 sigma), far stronger for V4-Pro than the report's 49. It takes the SM-to-chip table from the report and does not test the trained-weight trace, the AMD test or the GPU counts.

responses.t: Hacker News: DeepSeek already says its inference engine runs on SM100
responses.n: DeepSeek's DeepInfer (16 October 2026) lists NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 as supported hardware and benchmarks on SM100; its README confirms this (checked 27 November). Public evidence of Blackwell access for serving, not training.

responses.t: Hacker News: one Blackwell is enough to initialise a model
responses.n: The commonest objection: draw the weights on one developer's Blackwell, train elsewhere. The report states this limit itself; its own facts (Kimi K3's 64 seeded processes, MiniMax-M3's four seeded shards) point to initialising inside a sharded job, which weighs against one machine without excluding it.

responses.t: Hacker News: does Muon not erase the starting pattern?
responses.n: Asks how a starting pattern survives Muon, while granting the untouched rows are the strong evidence. The report's trained-layer figure is on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, trained with Muon for most matrices, and finds r 0.066: weak but measured.

responses.t: Defending the method on X (as reported)
responses.by: Will DePue, posts on X reported by HuggingNews
responses.n: Answers "initialised elsewhere" with K3's 64 Grace Blackwell processes and a 5 TB checkpoint nobody would move to save seconds, and "If labs initialized on one machine and trained on another I would not be 24 for 24." Says V4.1-Flash gave zero matches over 4.3 billion seeds (DeepSeek probably changed its initialisation) and Ascend's generators are untested. Known here only through this aggregator.

responses.t: Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer
responses.n: Typical coverage: the report's numbers and caveats, no outside expert, no comment from NVIDIA or the labs, and a headline saying "training" where the report says initialised; the author's own X thread likewise called the evidence "conclusive" for all four labs.

responses.t: gpu-forensics-hf: the replay as a tool for any Hugging Face model
responses.by: GitHub atripathy86 (a fork of the author's repository)
responses.n: A fork that finds untouched rows itself, recovers seeds, tests held-out rows and models the full launch rule; it lifts Ling-3.1-flash to r 0.99999 and reads DeepSeek-V2-Lite (A100) and Mistral-7B-v0.1 (seed 0, Hopper).

since.t: No reply from the labs or NVIDIA
since.n: By 27 November neither DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, Ant Group nor NVIDIA had commented in any source found; the full paper the author's thread promised was not out, and Unemployment Labs had published nothing else.

since.t: The Commerce Department's 16 November interim rule
since.n: Four days after the report, the US began requiring a licence to ship AI chips to any data centre, anywhere, that may serve Chinese companies (our 2026-11-23 issue). Renting Blackwell abroad, which the report could not exclude, is what that rule targets.

resources.t: PyTorch: DistributionTemplates.h (calc_execution_policy and the grid-stride kernel)
resources.n: Lines 49 to 61 set the grid to min(SMs times maxThreadsPerMultiProcessor / 256, the tensor's size / 256) blocks of 256 threads; lines 73 to 81 give thread idx Philox subsequence idx and its values at idx, idx + G, idx + 2G and so on. The whole fingerprint is in these 30 lines.

resources.t: Parallel Random Numbers: As Easy as 1, 2, 3 (Philox)
resources.by: Salmon, Moraes, Dror and Shaw, SC 2011 (maker)
resources.n: The counter-based generator behind cuRAND's Philox4x32-10: any thread can compute its own stream from (key, counter) with no shared state, which is why the numbers are identical on every chip and only their placement differs.
Supported hardware: NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950; benchmarks measured on SM100 GPUs. Independent of the forensics, and about serving, not training.

resources.t: Beyond the spy scandal: what the Nvidia Megaspeed case reveals about export controls
resources.n: Cited in the discussion thread for the legal point the report also makes: renting NVIDIA chips located outside China to Chinese companies did not, at the time, violate US export rules.

kb.t: GPU architecture: SMs, warps, tensor cores, Ampere to Blackwell and Rubin
kb.n: Owns SM counts per chip, which the fingerprint reads; it already carries a short note on this report.

kb.t: The CUDA programming model: threads, warps, blocks, launches, occupancy
kb.n: Grids, blocks and grid-stride loops: the launch shape whose total thread count is the fingerprint.

kb.t: Numerical computing for ML: floating point, precision formats, stable softmax
kb.n: BF16 rounding and why one computation gives different last bits on different hardware, the basis of the report's NVIDIA against AMD test.

kb.t: Making training fast: profiling, memory, attention, torchao
kb.n: Owns determinism and seeding: a seed alone does not reproduce a CUDA initialisation across GPUs with different SM counts.
What the starting weights are and why they are random normal values of a chosen spread.
V3 on H800s, V4 and V4.1-Flash: the lab with the clearest Hopper-to-Blackwell reading and one seed reused since 2024.
Kimi K2, K2.5 and K3: Hopper through K2.5, a 152-SM layout from K3.
M1 trained on 512 H800s; M3 reads as a 148-SM layout.
The map of chips, memory, interconnect and the building the report's GPU counts assume.
The issue that first linked the report.
The 16 November licence rule for data centres anywhere that may serve Chinese companies.
